## Abstract {.unnumbered}

After the M7.5 earthquake that struck coastal Venezuela on 24 June 2026, a large number of
satellite-derived building-damage products were released in the first days of the response.
We evaluated six damage classification products that were published and available within
the first ten days, from the technology sector, academia, the NGO community and the UN
system, against a reference dataset built from three sources: Copernicus EMS manually
mapped damage, an area-level crowd review (MapSwipe), and building-level field reports
(ChatMap).

No product supports acting on a single flagged building: baseline precision ran `{python} N["core_P_range2"]`
even in each product's most favourable region, and even under the most generous defensible
reading of the reference every product stays below `{python} N["P_upper_max"]`. The products do rank neighbourhoods well enough to triage, within a damage zone
that is already identified. The practical way to use them is to count agreement between
independent products. Flagging buildings at the better agreement thresholds roughly doubles the building-level performance (F1) of any single product, ranking neighbourhoods by three- or four-product agreement beats every single product's ranking (at both cell sizes tested), and the method needs no weights, training data or reference, so it can be run as soon as several products are in hand.

## The event, the products, and the references

An M7.5 earthquake struck the Venezuelan coast 20 km west of Catia La Mar at 22:05 UTC
on 24 June 2026, 32 seconds after an M7.2 inland near San Felipe, well to the west
(USGS events us6000t7zp and us6000t7zc; solutions as published on 10 September 2026).
Severe damage was concentrated along
the La Guaira coastal strip, in western Caracas, and in several inland towns. Copernicus
EMS rapid mapping was activated the same night (EMSR884). Products came from a variety
of organisations. The EU's rapid-mapping service, the Copernicus Emergency Management
Service (CEMS); a technology company, Microsoft AI for Good; universities, Oregon State
University working with NASA, and the University of Houston; an NGO, IMPACT Initiatives;
UN bodies, the United Nations Environment Programme / Office for the Coordination of
Humanitarian Affairs (UNEP/OCHA) Joint Environment Unit, the World Food Programme working
with the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology (LIST) and the European
Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN), and Data Insights for Social and
Humanitarian Action (DISHA), an initiative of UN Global Pulse; and a volunteer AI platform, the
Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team's fAIr. These products disagree with each other,
sometimes by a wide margin. A coordinator of search-and-rescue (SAR) teams receiving
several of them in the same week has no established way to decide which to trust, for
what purpose, and at what spatial scale.

We evaluate six damage classification products that were published and available within
the first ten days of the response (@tbl-products). A few products were excluded because
they had no accompanying area of analysis, or because the area they covered was too small
to support the comparison ([analysis extents](#app-regions) gives the specifics).
Throughout, a *flag* is a building a product marked as damaged to any extent.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-products
#| tbl-cap: "Damage products evaluated."
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, style, loc, md

from brief_numbers import N

# (product, provider, sensing basis, sensor and native resolution, key). Resolution as stated by the
# provider or visible in the delivery; "not stated" where neither applies — the gap is the point of the column.
P = [("Microsoft AI4G", "Microsoft", "VHR optical + AI classifier", "Vantor WorldView-3 and Planet SkySat scenes, sub-metre", "MS"),
     ("IMPACT v2", "IMPACT Initiatives", "Sentinel-1 radar backscatter amplitude change, intersected with building footprints (provider-confirmed)", "Sentinel-1, 10 m", "IMPACT"),
     ("OSU", "Oregon State Univ. / NASA", "Sentinel-1 radar coherence change", "Sentinel-1; product resolution not stated", "OSU"),
     ("UH QuakeDamage", "Univ. of Houston", "VHR optical (Vantor imagery, author-confirmed) + AI classifier grading every footprint", "Vantor, sub-metre", "UH"),
     ("LIST", "WFP / LIST / CERN", "AI change detection on before/after radar imagery (provider-stated)", "radar (sensor not stated); 10 m delivery grid", "LIST"),
     ("UNEP debris", "UNEP/OCHA JEU", "Sentinel-1 radar amplitude change detection on building footprints (debris tonnage modelled from the detected damage)", "Sentinel-1; product resolution not stated", "UNEP")]
rows = [dict(product=f"**{n}**<br><span style='font-size:11.5px;color:#666'>{pr}</span>", basis=b, sensor=s,
             scope=f'{N["scope_bld_" + k]} buildings · {N["scope_km2_" + k]} km²' if k != "UNEP" else "no published extent",
             flags=N["native_" + k]) for n, pr, b, s, k in P]
(GT(pd.DataFrame(rows))
 .fmt_markdown(columns=["product"])
 .cols_label(product="Product", basis="Sensing basis", sensor="Sensor and native resolution", scope="Analysis scope", flags="Damaged buildings flagged")
 .cols_align("right", columns=["flags"])
 .tab_source_note(md("Analysis scope counts Overture base buildings and area inside the provider's published extent. "
                     "Damaged buildings flagged is the provider's own count: its own footprints for Microsoft, UH and UNEP, base-building ids for IMPACT, OSU and LIST. "
                     "OSU figures refer to its v0 delivery, the version available during the response. UNEP publishes no extent and is scored under a stated coverage assumption. "
                     "Sensor and resolution are as stated by the provider or visible in the delivery; \"not stated\" marks the products for which neither applies."))
 .tab_style(style.text(color="#555", size="12px"), loc.body(columns=["provider", "basis", "sensor"]))
 .tab_options(table_font_size="13px", column_labels_font_weight="bold", data_row_padding="4px"))
```

![Product and analysis extents. Top: each provider's analysed extent and the CEMS-mapped
Copernicus EMS areas (dashed black). Bottom: the ~`{python} N["core_area_km2"]` km² area where all products
overlap (red), where every product can be evaluated against the same reference and
compared with the others. The paper calls this the core
region.](figures/fig_extents_map.png){#fig-extents}

We use two reporting regions throughout (@tbl-scope). *As delivered* evaluates each product
across the whole area it delivered, wherever that overlaps the CEMS-mapped areas. This is
the view that matches what responders actually received. The *core region* is the
~`{python} N["core_area_km2"]` km² where all six products and the reference overlap: one shared area where each
product can be compared against all the others. It holds `{python} N["cara_share_pct"]` of the
CEMS-recorded damage. The core region is the main scope for the rest of the paper; where a
section or caption uses the as-delivered frame instead, it says so.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-scope
#| tbl-cap: "The building-level scope of the two analysis frames used throughout this paper: as delivered, and the core region."
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, md, style, loc

from brief_numbers import N

K = [("Microsoft", "MS"), ("IMPACT v2", "IMPACT"), ("OSU", "OSU"), ("UH", "UH"), ("LIST", "LIST"), ("UNEP", "UNEP")]
rows = [dict(product=n, asd_b=N["asd_bld_" + k], asd_f=N["asd_flags_" + k], core_b=N["core_n_buildings"], core_f=N["core_flags_" + k]) for n, k in K]
(GT(pd.DataFrame(rows), rowname_col="product")
 .tab_spanner(label=md("**As delivered** (product-variable area)"), columns=["asd_b", "asd_f"])
 .tab_spanner(label=md(f'**Core region** ({N["core_area_km2"]} km²)'), columns=["core_b", "core_f"])
 .cols_label(asd_b="buildings", asd_f="flags", core_b="buildings", core_f="flags")
 .cols_align("right", columns=["asd_b", "asd_f", "core_b", "core_f"])
 .tab_style(style.fill("#e8f0f4"), loc.body(columns=["asd_b", "asd_f"]))
 .tab_style(style.fill("#f7e3e1"), loc.body(columns=["core_b", "core_f"]))
 .tab_source_note(md("Buildings: the Overture building footprints inside each area, the same base for every product. Flags: the buildings the product marked as damaged."))
 .tab_options(table_font_size="13px", column_labels_font_weight="bold", data_row_padding="4px"))
```

The reference dataset, against which every product is evaluated, is built from three
sources. They are used both to supplement one another and to evaluate one another.

The Copernicus EMS manually mapped damaged buildings are the most comprehensive building-level
source. The baseline reference is restricted to the buildings CEMS graded *damaged* or
*destroyed*: the strictest definition used in this study, though not the strictest
conceivable, since a destroyed-only reference would sit lower still, and the matching
convention pushes the other way (ADR-0034). Against these each
product's baseline precision and recall are set under one matching radius, applied from
both sides. For precision, a flagged building counts as a hit if a CEMS
damage point lies within 10 m of it; for recall, a CEMS damage point counts as found if a
flagged building lies within 10 m of it, so a miss is a CEMS point with no flag nearby.

From that baseline the performance calculations are extended in two ways, to give a range
of possible values rather than a single figure: by widening the reference to include the
buildings CEMS graded only *possibly damaged*, and by bringing in the two supplementary
sources.

MapSwipe is
a crowd review of ~50 m cells at locations AI products had flagged, by more than 400
volunteers: it can refute a false alarm but never reveal a miss, so it adjudicates disputed
flags and is never ground truth. ChatMap is `{python} N["field_n"]` damage reports from field
teams, positives-only with no survey frame: it can reveal misses but not false alarms
(the appendix [how MapSwipe and ChatMap were used](#app-reference) sets out how each is used). Because the reference is incomplete, every measured precision here is a
lower bound and every recall an upper bound.

## Results

### No product supports acting on a single flagged building {#sec-flags}

Building-level precision was low for every product. As delivered, precision across
everything the CEMS reference mapped ran from `{python} N["asd_P_min"]` (`{python} N["asd_P_min_product"]`) to `{python} N["asd_P_max"]` (`{python} N["asd_P_max_product"]`). Even
in the core region, where every product scores best, baseline precision reached only
`{python} N["core_P_range"]` against recall of `{python} N["core_R_range"]`: `{python} N["core_fa_per_hit_range"]` false alarms for
every hit, in the products' most favourable region and before any loosening of the reference. While the products do find damage, they also produce an enormous number of flags
with no reference record of damage underneath them. At this task a simple model of building
density and terrain performs in the same range ([the geography
benchmark](#app-null-brief)), so single-product flags should be treated as weak
evidence on their own.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-frames
#| tbl-cap: "Building-level precision and recall for each product, in the two analysis frames."
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, md, style, loc

from brief_numbers import rq5b as five, asd, PRODUCTS, LONG

rows = [dict(product=LONG[k],
             asd_p=f"{asd.loc[k]['P_cems']:.3f}", asd_r=f"{asd.loc[k]['R_cems']:.2f}",
             core_p=f"{five[10].loc[k]['P_cems']:.3f}", core_r=f"{five[10].loc[k]['R_cems']:.2f}")
        for k in PRODUCTS]
(GT(pd.DataFrame(rows), rowname_col="product")
 .tab_spanner(label=md("**As delivered**"), columns=["asd_p", "asd_r"])
 .tab_spanner(label=md("**Core region**"), columns=["core_p", "core_r"])
 .cols_label(asd_p="precision", asd_r="recall", core_p="precision", core_r="recall")
 .cols_align("right", columns=["asd_p", "asd_r", "core_p", "core_r"])
 .tab_style(style.fill("#e8f0f4"), loc.body(columns=["asd_p", "asd_r"]))
 .tab_style(style.fill("#f7e3e1"), loc.body(columns=["core_p", "core_r"]))
 .tab_source_note(md("Baseline reference (CEMS *damaged* or *destroyed*) at a 10 m matching radius. Precision is the share of a product's flags with reference damage underneath; recall the share of reference damage it flagged."))
 .tab_options(table_font_size="13px", column_labels_font_weight="bold", data_row_padding="4px"))
```

The area a provider chooses to analyse matters a great deal: the same product's
performance varies widely from region to region. Core-region numbers are each
product's favourable case; as delivered, the same product can be several times weaker
(UH: `{python} N["core_P_UH"]` in the core against `{python} N["asd_P_UH"]` across its delivery), because precision falls by
roughly the share of a product's flags placed in areas with little recorded damage
(@tbl-frames).

Those numbers come from the strictest configuration this study evaluates, and a defensible
one: a flag counts as correct only where a CEMS point graded *damaged* or *destroyed* lies
within 10 m of it. The study loosens that criterion in two ways: by raising the distance
threshold, and by relaxing the reference damage definition itself. Raising the threshold to
30 m lifts the best single product's precision to `{python} N["core_P30_max"]`
([performance versus matching radius](#app-radius) scores every product and rule at all
three distances).

Relaxing the reference itself is the more generous test, and @fig-bounds runs it using the
other reference data this study collected: first adding the points CEMS graded *possibly
damaged*, then instead crediting the flags the MapSwipe crowd reviewed and confirmed as
damaged, and finally both together. The result is a range of possible precision values per
product, with a realistic upper bound at the top. Even at that upper bound every product
stays below `{python} N["P_upper_max"]`. Neither loosening changes the conclusion: none of
these products is reliable enough to send a team to a single building it has flagged.

![Each product's precision under four reference
definitions, flags fixed, read left to right. Filled brown dot: the baseline, CEMS points graded
*damaged* or *destroyed*. Open circle: the reference widened to include points graded *possibly
damaged*. Open blue square: the baseline plus the flags the MapSwipe crowd reviewed and judged
damaged, an area-level check that can only raise precision ([how it works](#app-crowd)). Filled
blue diamond: both additions, the upper bound. ChatMap is left off the ladder because adding its
field points to the reference raises precision by only `{python} N["field_union_gain_range"]`
([how ChatMap was used](#app-chatmap)).](figures/rq2r_bounds_ladder.png){#fig-bounds}

These findings are in line with an [independent analysis](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/0f31285dcc4241d0a33f6ef768e16d1e) by the UN Global
Service Centre (UNGSC), which examined the same damage products and several others. It also found
individual products unreliable for identifying individual damaged buildings, and found wide
disagreement among the products.
<!-- placeholder: add a link to the UNGSC analysis paper here, beside the story map, once published -->

### The products rank neighbourhoods well enough to triage, within the damage zone {#sec-ranking}

The individual products do a much better job at ranking areas to prioritise than at
identifying specific damaged buildings. In the core region, subset to the area already known to be damaged,
every product orders ~`{python} N["h3_res8_km2"]` km² cells (H3 resolution 8) against the CEMS reference ordering achieving rank correlations
of `{python} N["rank_core8_range"]`, and the best single product (`{python} N["top20_single_product_8"]`) correctly identifies most of the twenty worst-hit cells (`{python} N["top20_single_8"]` of 20; no other product reaches half).

It is important to note that the ranking correlations deteriorate to
`{python} N["rank_asd7_range"]` when we look at the full as-delivered analysis level (@fig-ranktests).
The ranking value is really shown once the response has already narrowed down to a known
damage area. Without that subsetting, the products do not outperform a simple
[geography benchmark](#app-null-brief), so at this scale they are at best a supplementary
confirmation of it, not a way to find the damage zone.

Which product to trust is not knowable while it matters. Across the four contests in this
brief, building level and ranking in each of the two frames, there are three different
winners: `{python} N["core_P_best_product"]` has the highest building-level precision in the
core region and `{python} N["asd_P_max_product"]` as delivered, while `{python} N["rank_best_single"]`
ranks the core region best and `{python} N["rank_asd7_best"]` ranks best across full delivered
extents. `{python} N["core_P_best_product"]` moves from the best precision in the core region to
the weakest as delivered (`{python} N["core_P_UH"]` against `{python} N["asd_P_UH"]`). Every one of those
orderings was established against the CEMS reference weeks after the response needed it.

![Each product's Spearman rank correlation with the CEMS reference ordering, across both
analysis levels, at the two H3 resolutions used to define neighbourhood
areas.](figures/rq3f_null_ranking_both_summary.png){#fig-ranktests}

### Count agreement between products {#sec-dial}

The more products agree on a building, the more likely its flag is real, because each
product's false alarms fall in different places. The number required to agree is a
threshold a responder/analyst can set. Flag every building any product marked and `{python} N["k1_R_pct"]` of
known damage is covered, but a field team following those flags would make `{python} N["k1_visits10_int"]` site
visits for each confirmed damaged building; require all six to agree and `{python} N["k6_P_pct"]` of flags
are correct but only `{python} N["k6_R_pct"]` of the damage is covered. Between the extremes, each added
agreeing product raises the odds that a flag is real, and setting the threshold fixes
the size of the field job the same day (@tbl-dial). Setting the threshold fixes how
many buildings field teams will visit; it does not fix how many of them will turn out
damaged.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-dial
#| tbl-cap: "The agreement dial: what each threshold costs and buys, core region. Share of flags correct and share of known damage covered at 10 m; visits per find at 30 m."
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, html
from brief_numbers import rq5b as five, N_CEMS_CORE as N_CEMS

rows = []
for k in range(1, 7):
    key = f"{k}-of-6"; r10 = five[10].loc[key]; r30 = five[30].loc[key]
    rows.append(dict(rule=f"{k} of 6", flags=f"{int(r10['flagged']):,}",
                     P=f"{100 * r10['P_cems']:.0f}%", R=f"{100 * r10['R_cems']:.0f}%",
                     visits=f"{r10['flagged'] / (r30['R_cems'] * N_CEMS):.1f}"))
(GT(pd.DataFrame(rows), rowname_col="rule")
 .cols_label(flags="buildings flagged", P=html("share of flags<br>correct"), R=html("share of known<br>damage covered"), visits=html("field visits<br>per find"))
 .cols_align("right", columns=["flags", "P", "R", "visits"])
 .tab_options(column_labels_font_weight="bold", table_font_size="13.5px", data_row_padding="5px"))
```

Weight the count toward products that *fail differently*. Scoring all `{python} N["pair_n"]` two-product
rules in this event (@fig-frontier), the `{python} N["pair_radar_n"]` pairs built from two radar products added
the least (precision `{python} N["pair_radar_P_range"]`), and every pair above a precision of `{python} N["pair_P_thresh"]` contained
one of the two high-resolution optical products. The best pair mixed an optical and a
radar product (`{python} N["pair_best"]`, `{python} N["pair_P_best"]`); the next best paired the two optical products,
which share a sensor class but not a method (`{python} N["pair_second"]`, `{python} N["pair_P_second"]`). Sensor
alone does not predict which pair will work, and one event cannot settle it: treat this
as a reason to mix sensing methods, not as a ranking of providers.

![The six products as shipped (grey), all `{python} N["pair_n"]` two-product agreement rules (open
circles, labelled) and the six k-of-6 rules (blue squares, k inside), in the core region. Precision
and recall are measured against CEMS points graded *damaged* or *destroyed*, matched within 10 m;
whiskers run from measured to crowd-adjusted precision. Pairs of two radar products sit lowest; pairs
that include a high-resolution optical product sit highest.](figures/rq5b_frontier_r10.png){#fig-frontier}

Counting agreement is also close to the ceiling of what any combination can achieve. A
statistically fitted combination of the six products scores about `{python} N["fusion_over_vote_pct"]` higher on F1 than counting, both scored on the building labels the model is fitted to (`{python} N["fusion_over_vote_pct_nested"]` when its cutoff is chosen without sight of the test data), but
fitting it requires the damage map a responder is still waiting for, so it explains the
event afterwards and cannot run during one; flat counting can be done as soon as
several products are in hand (@fig-bestf1).

![F1 at each product's own threshold, at both analysis levels, beside the best of the six
agreement rules (green), which exists only in the core region. Bar labels give F1, precision
and recall, counted as in @tbl-frames.](figures/best_f1_points_r10.png){#fig-bestf1}

Counting agreement helps the area ranking too, not just the building-level decision
(@fig-agreerank). Ranking cells by their count of buildings with three or four products agreeing beats every
single product's ordering (ρ `{python} N["rank_best_vote_rho"]` against the best single's `{python} N["rank_best_single_rho"]` at ~`{python} N["h3_res8_km2"]` km² cells),
and for a shortlist, "which 20 cells first", high agreement is clearly better:
the best agreement rule shortlists `{python} N["top20_vote_8"]` of the 20 worst-hit cells against the best single
product's `{python} N["top20_single_8"]`, and `{python} N["top20_vote_9"]` against `{python} N["top20_single_9"]` at the finer scale.

![Rank correlations (top) of each product (grey) at two block scales (left and right)
against the combined product at different k-of-6 agreement configurations (green). The
bottom row shows the percentage of the 20 worst-hit neighbourhood blocks also identified
as the worst 20, for each product and each combined
configuration.](figures/rq3h_agreement_ranking_summary.png){#fig-agreerank}

::: {.rec}
[Coordinators]{.rec-who}

The coordination has to come before the analysis. Everything the procedure above asks for
was assembled during and after the response rather than being in place before it: a common
building base, each product's analysed extent, the agreement count across products. It should be standing
infrastructure that runs as deliveries arrive, with a shared picture of who has analysed
where, a consolidation point that receives products against a stated template (analysed
extent, metadata, a common basemap and footprint set), and the combination produced
automatically rather than by a retrospective study.
:::

::: {.rec}
[Providers]{.rec-who}

Publish an analysed extent; without one, a user cannot tell "no flag" from "not
analysed", so the product cannot be fairly evaluated or confidently used. Publish the
sensor and its native spatial resolution alongside the method.
Publish per-building acquisition metadata (scene count and dates). Where the product is
delivered on its own building footprints, publish those footprints and say where they came
from, so a user can map them onto whatever base they are working with. Where the method
produces a confidence value, publish it, along with a clear statement of how it was
derived and what it means. And accept feedback during the activation: a crowd campaign
rejected `{python} N["r1_no_share_pct"]` of one zone's flagged locations within days, and there was no mechanism for returning that
result to the provider while reprocessing could still help.
:::

::: {.rec}
[Analysts supporting the response]{.rec-who}

Someone has to turn several disagreeing products into something a responder can act on.
This is the procedure this evaluation supports for the first days, when products arrive
with very different extents.

1. **Establish the worst-hit zone from shaking and exposure, not from the products.**
   Triangulate a shaking model and building density with field and media reports. Ranking
   a product across its full delivered scope may support or contradict that picture, but
   it cannot establish it: at that scale a simple
   [geography benchmark](#app-null-brief) ranked these areas better than all six products.
2. **Narrow to that zone before using the products for triage.** Every ranking result
   here holds inside a zone already known to be damaged and weakens outside it
   (@sec-ranking).
3. **Do not spend the first days choosing a product.** Which one is strongest changes
   with the task and the area, and was only established against the CEMS reference
   weeks later (@sec-ranking).
4. **Count agreement instead.** Counting needs no weights, no training data and no
   reference, so it runs as soon as several products are in hand. Two are not enough on
   their own: the fifteen possible pairs here ranged from `{python} N["pair_P_worst"]` to
   `{python} N["pair_P_best"]` in precision depending on which two. Weight the count toward
   products with independent sensing methods (@sec-dial).
5. **Rank at several agreement levels rather than one.** The best level is no more
   knowable in advance than the best product: here `{python} N["rank_best_vote"]` ranked
   cells best while `{python} N["top20_vote_rule_8"]` shortlisted the worst 20 best
   (@fig-agreerank). Read them together, and set the acting threshold from @tbl-dial
   against the field team's capacity.

Steps 2 to 5 rest on core-region results: the agreement rules were never scored across
full delivered extents. When reporting what you find, a single CEMS reference
understates precision where damage is lighter: publish measured precision as a lower
bound, or adjudicate the disputed flags against a second reference and publish the
interval.
:::

::: {.rec}
[Responders]{.rec-who}

Expect several damage products within days of an earthquake, covering different areas by
different methods, and disagreeing with each other.

Where other sources already point to the worst-hit zone, shaking, exposure, field and
media reports, it is reasonable to expect most of these products to rank neighbourhoods
usefully *inside* that zone in the first 72 hours. None of them is a reliable way to find
the zone in the first place, and no product evaluated here supports acting on an
individual flagged building.

What the analysis should hand you is not one organisation's map but a count: for each
building, how many independent products flagged it. Read that count as a confidence
level. The more products agree, the more likely the flag is real damage and the fewer
buildings you are sent to. @tbl-dial gives, at each level of agreement, how many
buildings are flagged, what share of them are really damaged, and how many visits each
confirmed find costs. Ask for the level that matches what your teams can actually visit.

This evaluation cannot see what you already have. A responder with local knowledge, field
reporting or ground access may be able to use a single product sensibly in ways the
numbers here cannot anticipate; what the numbers can say is what the products support on
their own. Nothing currently available sees lighter damage reliably, so plan shelter
assessments accordingly.

:::

## Limitations

This is one event, one geography, and mostly one damage zone: a single earthquake
in a coastal, dense-urban setting, and the core comparison region is only ~`{python} N["core_area_km2"]` km², with
`{python} N["cara_share_pct"]` of the CEMS reference in a single AOI (Caraballeda). The specific rule orderings
and magnitudes are hypotheses elsewhere until replicated.

The references have limits of their own, and the largest was measured rather than
assumed: the CEMS reference captured `{python} N["cems_field_complete_pct"]` of field-reported destroyed buildings but only
`{python} N["cems_field_significant_pct"]` of those significantly damaged ([how MapSwipe and ChatMap were used](#app-reference)),
which is why every precision here is a lower bound and every recall an upper bound. The
crowd campaign was seeded almost entirely on Microsoft's flags, so it scrutinises products very
unevenly and can never see any product's misses; the field reports are undated, positives-only,
skewed toward destruction, and come with no defined collection area.

## Appendix {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="Show the full appendix"}

### Analysis extents {#app-regions .unnumbered}

| reporting region | what it is | used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Core region** | the ~`{python} N["core_area_km2"]` km² intersection of the CEMS extents with all five extent-publishing products (@fig-extents): one shared cell set | voting, the pairwise rules, fusion, and the best-F1 geography comparison |
| **As delivered** | each product's full delivered footprint, wherever CEMS mapped: a different region per product | as-delivered precision and recall, and the geography benchmark; ranking test 1 |

: The two reporting regions. Sections and captions state which they use. The core
region gives every predictor an identical cell set (one geography score); as-delivered
is per-product by design, so the geography model is re-scored on each product's own
footprint there. {#tbl-regions}

- UNEP and UH published no extents, and are handled differently. UNEP flagged buildings in every
  CEMS-mapped area, so it is treated as covering them. UH's extent is the polygon around its
  own classified footprints, which does not reach every CEMS-mapped area: it has no flags in
  San Felipe.
- Two products in the same window are not evaluated. HOT's fAIr published no extent, so its
  misses cannot be counted. DISHA published one, but it covers `{python} N["disha_share_pct"]` of the core
  region and holds `{python} N["disha_cems"]` of its `{python} N["core_cems"]` CEMS damage points; admitting it
  would have halved the shared comparison area.

### How performance was measured {#app-matching .unnumbered}

- The product and the reference have different geometries, so there is no shared instance list
  and no single confusion matrix. Scoring is by proximity.
- Precision anchors on the product, recall on the reference, each with its own denominator.
  Neither uses the undamaged background, so its size affects no score.
- A product is accountable only where it and the reference both looked, so scoring is restricted
  to the intersection of analysed extents.

```{python}
#| label: fig-matching
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "Counting hits, false alarms and misses. Left: a product is scored only where it and the reference both looked. Middle: each CEMS damage point is checked for a product flag within radius r, which gives recall. Right: each flagged building is checked for a CEMS point within r, which gives precision."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mp
import numpy as np
from shapely.geometry import Point

R = 0.16
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 2.95))   # drawn at about the appendix column's width   # stacked: side by side ran past the page margin
a0 = ax[0]
c1, c2 = Point(-0.28, 0).buffer(0.75), Point(0.28, 0).buffer(0.75)
inter = c1.intersection(c2)
a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(inter.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="#c8e6c9", ec="none"))
for c, col, lab, xy in ((c1, "tab:blue", "CEMS\nextent", (-0.98, 0.55)),
                        (c2, "tab:orange", "product\nextent", (0.5, 0.55))):
    a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(c.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="none", ec=col, lw=2))
    a0.annotate(lab, xy, fontsize=8, color=col)
a0.annotate("scored\nhere only", (0, -0.1), fontsize=8.5, ha="center", weight="bold", color="#2e7d32")
a0.set_title("1 · where scoring\nhappens", fontsize=9)
a1 = ax[1]
for x, y in [(-0.38, 0.22), (0.05, -0.32), (-0.6, -0.5), (0.62, -0.15)]:
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.3, True), (0.15, -0.25, True), (0.45, 0.42, False)]:
    a1.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
    a1.annotate("TP" if hit else "FN (missed)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=7.5,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a1.set_title("2 · recall: check\neach CEMS point", fontsize=9)
a2 = ax[2]
for x, y in [(-0.36, 0.25), (0.2, -0.14)]:
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.32, True), (0.1, -0.2, True), (0.5, 0.45, False), (-0.15, -0.6, False)]:
    a2.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
    a2.annotate("TP" if hit else "FP (false\nalarm)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=7.5,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a2.set_title("3 · precision: check\neach product flag", fontsize=9)
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(-1.05, 1.05); a.set_ylim(-1.0, 0.9)
    a.set_aspect("equal"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
h = [plt.Line2D([], [], marker="*", ls="", ms=13, c="k", label="CEMS damage point"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", ms=8, c="tab:orange", label="product-flagged building"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], ls="--", c="grey", label="match radius r")]
fig.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.09, 1, 0.98))
plt.show()
```

- Products that delivered their own footprints are mapped onto the shared building base by one
  rule: highest overlap, else nearest within 20 m, else no match. 
- The matching radius chosen comes from the building spacing: the median distance between
  neighbouring buildings in the core region is `{python} N["spacing_median_m"]` m, and
  `{python} N["spacing_within20_pct"]` have a neighbour within 20 m.
- Radii other than 10 m are used for two different purposes. Against ChatMap a more generous 20 m
  is applied, to account for the GPS uncertainty in field-reported points. And 30 m is a *finding
  distance*, close enough that a responder sent to a flag could plausibly find the damaged
  building: it is what the coverage and visits-per-find columns of @tbl-dial report. Both radii are
  also swept as sensitivity tests in [sensitivity to the matching radius](#app-radius).
- Reference grades: *damaged* and *destroyed* count, *possibly damaged* does not. What happens
  when that choice is relaxed is in [building-level performance against the benchmark](#app-null-building).

[]{#app-reference}

[]{#app-crowd}

**How MapSwipe was used.** MapSwipe turns the single precision figure measured against CEMS into
a range. A flag with no CEMS point near it counts as a false alarm, but a gap in the reference and
a genuine false alarm look the same. MapSwipe is a HOT volunteer platform, and in this event its
volunteers reviewed ~50 m cells for visible damage, which separates the two wherever they looked.

- The first campaign was built to review Microsoft's flags, with a few dozen cells from HOT's fAIr,
  so it is not spread evenly across the products. The others are covered only where their flags
  happen to fall inside cells drawn for Microsoft. Coverage of each product's unmatched flags runs
  from `{python} N["crowdcov_MS"]` for Microsoft and `{python} N["crowdcov_UNEP"]` for UNEP down to
  `{python} N["crowdcov_OSU"]` for OSU and `{python} N["crowdcov_UH"]` for UH, so the adjustment says the most about
  Microsoft and the least about UH.
- The crowd only re-judges product flags that have no CEMS point within 10 m, which would otherwise
  count as false alarms. If most volunteers who saw that flag's cell said damaged, the flag counts as
  a hit; if they said no or not sure, or never saw the cell, it stays a false alarm. Flags a CEMS
  point already confirms are never re-judged, and neither are buildings a product did not flag, so
  the crowd can raise precision but never lower it, and leaves recall alone.
- When crowd-adjusted precision is used in the paper, the CEMS-only precision is the bottom of the
  range and the crowd-adjusted value sits above it.

![How the MapSwipe crowd enters the precision calculation. Hexagons are the ~50 m crowd task
cells in Catia La Mar, tinted by majority verdict. A flag matched by a CEMS point within 10 m
is a true positive and the crowd plays no part (green). An unmatched flag in a cell the crowd
judged damaged is counted as confirmed and improves the adjusted precision (blue). In a cell
judged undamaged or uncertain it stays a false alarm (orange), and a flag in a cell nobody voted
on earns nothing.](figures/rq7_crowd_adjustment_explainer_r1.png){#fig-crowdmech}

- Every crowd-adjusted number in this brief comes from this first round. A second campaign re-voted
  the same cells in August 2026, after the numbers were frozen, with about sixteen votes per cell
  instead of six. Swapping its verdicts in moves each product's crowd-adjusted precision by at most
  `{python} N["r2_padj_maxdelta"]`, and no product overtakes another.

[]{#app-chatmap}

**How ChatMap was used.** ChatMap field teams reported damaged buildings from the ground,
independently of any satellite imagery, which makes it one dataset that can check the CEMS
reference itself.

- CEMS captured `{python} N["cems_field_complete_pct"]` of field-reported destroyed buildings but only
  `{python} N["cems_field_significant_pct"]` of those significantly damaged, and every product shows the
  same slope.

![ChatMap field reports are an independent dataset that helps evaluate both the products and
the CEMS reference. Each line is one dataset's recall against those reports, at complete
destruction versus significant damage. Every line slopes the same way: destruction is
found far more often than damage, the products and the CEMS reference
alike.](figures/rq2e_grade_slope.png){#fig-gradeslope}

- ChatMap can also be added to the reference directly, since its points are building-level.
  However, doing so raises measured precision minimally, by roughly
  `{python} N["field_union_gain_range"]`, and it has not been included in the main text.
- Recall against ChatMap is matched at 20 m rather than 10 m due to uncertainty in the accuracy of spatial information provided by ChatMap.

### The geography benchmark {#app-null-brief .unnumbered}

#### How the benchmark is built {#app-null-build .unnumbered} 

- Every product is compared against a deliberately simple benchmark that uses no satellite imagery:
  modelled shaking intensity, plus the vulnerability of the setting proxied by building density and
  by terrain slope and elevation.
- It is fitted with hindsight to this event's own damage labels and validated on spatial blocks it
  never trained on. Its inputs are available on day zero anywhere; its coefficients are not. It is a
  benchmark, not an operational alternative.
- Validation is by spatial blocking: the map is cut into ~`{python} N["h3_res7_km2"]` km² zones and the model
  is always scored on zones it never trained on, because neighbouring buildings resemble each other
  in both features and damage.
- It is fitted two ways, a logistic regression and a random forest, and both are reported. Every
  paired comparison in this brief uses the logistic, so the whole brief rests on one model, even
  though the forest is marginally stronger at building level in the core region
  (`{python} N["null_rf_F1"]` against `{python} N["null_F1"]`).

![How the geography benchmark is built](figures/rq8_dayzero_schematic.png){#fig-dayzero-build}

#### Building-level performance against the benchmark {#app-null-building .unnumbered}

![Precision of each product, the two composite combinations and the geography benchmark under three
definitions of the CEMS reference. The vertical dashed line marks the paper's common reference definition.](figures/rq8c_basis_precision_r10.png){#fig-basis}

- Widening the grade definition lifts every precision by `{python} N["possibly_lift_range"]`. But the
  key findings stay largely the same: the combinations
  stay well above every single product, and the geography benchmark stays inside the products' band
  under every definition.

#### Area ranking against the benchmark {#app-ranking-tables .unnumbered}

- The same benchmark test applied to ranking: sum the model's predicted per-building risk over the
  same cells, which needs no threshold, and correlate with the CEMS count (@fig-nullrank).

![Each product's rank correlation with the
CEMS damage ordering, beside the geography benchmark scored on the same cells. As delivered the
benchmark is re-scored on each product's own footprint overlap with CEMS reference, so it takes a different value per row;
in the core region every predictor shares one cell set, so it has a single score, drawn as the
vertical rule.](figures/rq3f_null_ranking_both.png){#fig-nullrank}

- Across the delivered footprints geography ranks these areas better than the products do, beating
  `{python} N["null_beats_n_asd7"]` of six at the coarser scale, with large margins.

- Within the known damage zone, the core region, the individual products rank much better than
  across their full delivered scope.
- So the products do know where within a damaged area to go first. What they do not add is which
  area that is, which is the part geography already encodes.
- The geography benchmark is fitted with hindsight to the known damage labels, so it is not a viable
  alternative in real time. Its purpose here is solely as an informative benchmark.

![Each product's rank correlation with the
CEMS ordering across its delivered footprint, when cells are ranked by damaged-building count (filled circles, the
paper's target) versus damage fraction (filled squares; cells with at least 20
buildings). Open markers: the geography benchmark under each target. The benchmark is as strong
under fractions as under counts, and only OSU beats it under
either.](figures/rq3g_frac_vs_count_rho.png){#fig-fracrank}

- Ranking by damage fraction instead of count moves some products up and others down, but the
  benchmark is as strong either way.

### Additional tests {#app-tests .unnumbered}

#### Sensitivity to the matching radius {#app-radius .unnumbered}

- Throughout the paper the common radius used is 10 m. Here we test at 20 m and at 30 m.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-dial-full
#| tbl-cap: "Building-level performance in full: the six products and the six agreement rules in the core region at matching radii of 10, 20 and 30 m. Parentheses at 10 m give each product's as-delivered value. Crowd-adjusted precision re-judges CEMS-unmatched flags against the crowd verdicts, credited only where volunteers reviewed the cell; crowd reviewed is the share of each row's unmatched flags they saw. Visits per find is field visits per damage point reached at 30 m. Shading ranks values within each column."
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, html, style, loc
from matplotlib import colormaps
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex

from brief_numbers import rq5b as five, asd   # both slices of artefacts/results.csv

products = ["MS", "IMPACT", "OSU", "UH", "LIST", "UNEP"]
rules = [f"{k}-of-6" for k in range(1, 7)]
labels = {"MS": "Microsoft", "IMPACT": "IMPACT v2"}
from brief_numbers import N_CEMS_CORE as N_CEMS

disp, nums = [], []
for key in products + rules:
    d = {"rule": labels.get(key, key),
         "group": "Products" if key in products else "Voting rules (k of 6 agree)"}
    n = {}
    d["flags"] = f"{int(five[10].loc[key]['flagged']):,}"
    for r in (10, 20, 30):
        row = five[r].loc[key]
        for m, ml in (("P_cems", "P"), ("R_cems", "R"), ("F1_cems", "F1")):
            col = f"{ml}{r}"
            n[col] = float(row[m])
            if r == 10 and key in products and m in ("P_cems", "R_cems"):
                d[col] = f"{row[m]:.3f} ({float(asd.loc[key][m]):.3f})"
            else:
                d[col] = f"{row[m]:.3f}"
    n["Padj"] = float(five[10].loc[key]["P_crowd"])
    _cov = five[10].loc[key]["crowd_cov_of_fps"]
    d["Padj"] = f"{n['Padj']:.3f}"
    d["cov"] = f"{100 * _cov:.0f}%"   # coverage in its own column, so parentheses in this table mean "as delivered" only
    visits = five[10].loc[key]["flagged"] / (five[30].loc[key]["R_cems"] * N_CEMS)
    n["visits"] = -visits
    d["visits"] = f"{visits:.1f}"
    disp.append(d); nums.append(n)

cols = ["rule", "flags", "P10", "R10", "F110", "Padj", "cov",
        "P20", "R20", "F120", "P30", "R30", "F130", "visits"]
df = pd.DataFrame(disp)[["group"] + cols]
nm = pd.DataFrame(nums)[[c for c in cols if c not in ("rule", "flags", "cov")]]   # cov is not shaded

cmap = colormaps["Blues"]
gt = (GT(df, rowname_col="rule", groupname_col="group")
      .tab_spanner("10 m", ["P10", "R10", "F110", "Padj", "cov"])
      .tab_spanner("20 m", ["P20", "R20", "F120"])
      .tab_spanner("30 m", ["P30", "R30", "F130", "visits"])
      .cols_label(flags="flags", P10="P", R10="R", F110="F1", Padj=html("P<br>(crowd-adj)"), cov=html("crowd<br>reviewed"),
                  P20="P", R20="R", F120="F1", P30="P", R30="R", F130="F1",
                  visits=html("visits<br>per find"))
      .tab_options(column_labels_font_weight="bold",
                   row_group_font_weight="bold",
                   table_font_size="13px",
                   data_row_padding="4px"))
for col in nm.columns:
    vals = nm[col]
    lo, hi = vals.min(), vals.max()
    for i, v in enumerate(vals):
        t = 0.0 if hi == lo else (v - lo) / (hi - lo)
        gt = gt.tab_style(style.fill(color=to_hex(cmap(0.15 + 0.55 * t))),
                          loc.body(columns=[col], rows=[i]))
gt
```

- Every number rises with the radius, because a flag one or two buildings away starts to count.
- The benchmark gains fastest: a wider radius spreads each CEMS point over a cluster of neighbours,
  making the target area-shaped, which is the shape a smooth spatial predictor captures well.
- Combination stays ahead at every radius, so the findings hold whichever radius is used.
- The tighter 10 m label concentrates the positives onto individual buildings, which is where the
  case for combining products is strongest, and it is the reading in which a building-level claim
  means a building.
- The cloud check: only Microsoft publishes per-building visibility, and scored against it the effect
  is negligible. The model abstains under cloud rather than flagging into it.

#### Bootstrapped confidence intervals {#app-ci .unnumbered}

- Every interval is a 95% spatial block bootstrap: hexagonal cells resampled with replacement 2,000
  times, each statistic recomputed from the frozen match indicators.
- The same cell draw is shared by every predictor, so differences between predictors are paired.
  Nothing is refitted inside the loop, so the intervals measure sampling noise around the reported
  numbers, not a re-run of the threshold search.
- Because whole neighbourhoods are resampled the intervals are wide: one damage cluster entering or
  leaving the sample moves a product's precision by more than its decimals suggest.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ci-core
#| tbl-cap: "Core region, 95% block-bootstrap intervals, counted as in the main text (recall is the share of CEMS points found). P/R/F1 at 10 m, crowd-adjusted precision (10 m), F1 at 30 m, and visits per find (30 m). The 20 m radius and the as-delivered region are in the frozen artefact (RQ9)."
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT

from brief_numbers import ci   # rq9 core intervals, from artefacts/results.csv
def cell(rule, radius, metric, dp=3):
    r = ci[(ci["rule"] == rule) & (ci.radius == radius) & (ci.metric == metric)].iloc[0]
    f = f"{{:.{dp}f}}"
    return f"{f.format(r['point'])} ({f.format(r['lo'])}–{f.format(r['hi'])})"

order = ["MS", "IMPACT", "OSU", "UH", "LIST", "UNEP"] + [f"{k}-of-6" for k in range(1, 7)]
labels = {"MS": "Microsoft", "IMPACT": "IMPACT v2"}
rows = [{"rule": labels.get(k, k),
         "P10": cell(k, 10, "P"), "R10": cell(k, 10, "R"), "F110": cell(k, 10, "F1"),
         "Padj": cell(k, 10, "P_crowd"), "F130": cell(k, 30, "F1"),
         "visits": cell(k, 30, "visits_per_find", dp=1)} for k in order]
(GT(pd.DataFrame(rows), rowname_col="rule")
 .tab_spanner("10 m", ["P10", "R10", "F110", "Padj"])
 .tab_spanner("30 m", ["F130", "visits"])
 .cols_label(P10="P", R10="R", F110="F1", Padj="P (crowd-adj)", F130="F1",
             visits="visits/find")
 .tab_options(column_labels_font_weight="bold", table_font_size="12.5px",
              data_row_padding="3px"))
```

### Product updates {#app-updates .unnumbered}

- Three providers released later versions of their products after the response: Microsoft, OSU and
  UH. None of them is a focus of this evaluation. The brief scores what was available in the first
  weeks, which is what responders actually had.
- Microsoft's later version: **TBD.**
- UH's later version: **TBD.**
- OSU's second version was evaluated, and the result is the same shape. It turned over more than
  half the flag list and moved precision and recall barely at all (`{python} N["osu_v0_P"]` to
  `{python} N["osu_v1_P"]` precision). We score the first version throughout, because that is what
  responders had; the operational dashboard now uses the second.
- A revision that relabels half the buildings without moving either metric is itself evidence that
  at the individual-building level these products are noise-dominated. Version-to-version stability
  belongs beside accuracy when judging them. The area-level signal is robust to that churn.
- That version's certainty tiers are correctly ordered, and the high-confidence cut is its best
  operating point, but it remains below Microsoft's core-region precision and far below the
  agreement rules.

:::
